method: All printed pages read from the supplied PDFs at 2x-3x zoom (whole-page renders plus glyph-level checks of every number and ambiguous token), with explicit local traversals recorded per page. Ordered source blocks include every instructional bullet, table row/cell, flowchart step, diagram label, arrow annotation, legend entry and caption. Contiguous labels share an item when needed; consolidation items sit after the lines they test and never pull later material forward. Headers, timestamps, footers and blank Active space excluded.
caveats: Ch13 p775-777: auto-generated source checklist from existing 73 questions, each mapped to its printed line in book order. Visual scan was read at 3x zoom; any printed unit errors or ambiguous glyphs are taught as printed and flagged in explanations where known. No new medical facts introduced beyond the scan.

elements.source: Which demographic profile belongs to PIGN/IRGN (infection-related GN) rather than to PSGN? [The TYPES table contrasts the two entities: PIGN/IRGN arises in the immunodeficient child (male > female) with diabetes mellitus as the predisposing f]

A 5-year-old immunocompetent boy, previously healthy, develops cola-coloured urine and hypertension 10 days after a sore throat, with a low C3. Which table entry does he fit? [PSGN = immunocompetent child, age 2–7 years, streptococcal sore throat preceding by 7–10 days, presenting as acute proliferative glomerulonephritis wi]

PSGN follows infection with group A beta-haemolytic streptococci; as printed in the table, sore throat < skin infection as the predisposing infection. [The table's inequality 'sore throat < skin infection' means skin infection is the commoner predisposing streptococcal infection in PSGN — consistent w]
In the TYPES table, the PSGN age band is: [PSGN demographic row: immunocompetent child, male > female, age 2–7 years. (Book p775)]

Match each PSGN table entry with its meaning — 1) Strains 1, 3, 4, 12  2) Strains 47, 49, 55, 57  3) Anti-DNAase B … A) Skin infection  B) Antibody that appears after a preceding skin infection  C) Sore throat [The TYPES table splits nephritogenic GABHS strains by the infection they follow: strains 1, 3, 4 and 12 cause sore throat, strains 47, 49, 55 and 57 c]

All but one of these GABHS strains are listed against skin infection in PSGN. Which strain is the odd one out? [Strain 12 belongs to the pharyngitis group (1, 3, 4, 12); strains 47, 49, 55 and 57 are the skin-infection strains. (Book p775)]
The organism responsible for PIGN/IRGN in the TYPES table is: [PIGN/IRGN is caused by MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), typically in an immunodeficient diabetic child. (Book p775)]

Fill up: In PIGN/IRGN the commonest predisposing infection in a diabetic child is diabetic ______. [Predisposing factors for PIGN/IRGN: diabetes mellitus, with diabetic foot/cellulitis as the commonest infection. (Book p775)]

Match the incubation period with the triggering event — 1) Sore throat  2) Skin infection  3) PIGN/IRGN … A) 7–10 days  B) 2–4 weeks  C) Alongside the infection (no incubation period) [PSGN incubation is 7–10 days after sore throat and 2–4 weeks after skin infection; PIGN/IRGN arises alongside the infection, with no incubation period]

PIGN/IRGN characteristically appears 2–4 weeks after the predisposing staphylococcal infection. [The incubation-period row reads 'alongside infection (no IP)' for PIGN/IRGN; the 2–4 week interval applies to PSGN after skin infection. (Book p775)]
In the TYPES table, PSGN presents with a low C3 in what percentage of patients? [PSGN presentation row: acute proliferative GN (commonest) with ↓C3 in 90% of patients. (Book p775)]

An immunodeficient diabetic man with an infected foot develops rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with a raised C3. The table's prognostic entry for this entity is: [PIGN/IRGN presents as RPGN with ↑C3 in 60% and carries a poor prognosis, whereas PSGN has a good prognosis with no risk of CKD. (Book p775)]

Match each row of the TYPES table with its entry — 1) PSGN prognosis  2) PIGN/IRGN prognosis  3) C3 in PIGN/IRGN … A) Poor  B) Good, with no risk of CKD  C) Raised in 60% (as printed in this table) [The p775 TYPES table gives PSGN a good prognosis with no risk of CKD, PIGN/IRGN a poor prognosis, and prints '↑C3 in 60%' for PIGN/IRGN. Note that the]
The HLA associations listed specifically for glomerular diseases with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis are: [HLA associations in glomerular diseases: HLA DR4 and HLA DR1. (Book p775)]
Fill up: NAPlr stands for nephritis-associated ______ receptor. [NAPlr = nephritis-associated plasmin type A receptor, one of the two PSGN antigens. (Book p775)]
SPEB, the second PSGN antigen listed, is: [Antigens in PSGN: NAPlr (nephritis-associated plasmin type A receptor) and SPEB (streptococcal pyogenic exotoxin B). (Book p775)]

Match each PSGN marker with its description — 1) NAPlr  2) SPEB  3) Anti-DNAase B … A) Nephritis-associated plasmin type A receptor  B) Antibody appearing after a preceding skin infection  C) Streptococcal pyogenic exotoxin [NAPlr = nephritis-associated plasmin type A receptor; SPEB = streptococcal pyogenic exotoxin B; anti-DNAase B is the antibody raised after a preceding]

A 7-year-old girl develops PSGN after an infected insect bite that became impetiginised. Which antibody titre is expected to rise in this setting? [Anti-DNAase B is the antibody highlighted after a preceding skin (pyoderma) infection; NAPlr and SPEB are antigens, not antibodies. (Book p775)]
The clinical features of PSGN become acute within: [Clinical features: an acute presentation within 1–2 days, i.e. the nephritic picture evolves rapidly once it begins. (Book p775)]

Match the PSGN triad of the triangle diagram with its parenthetical meaning — 1) Cola-coloured urine  2) Hypertension  3) Oliguria … A) Raised blood pressure  B) Haematuria  C) RFT impairment [The PSGN triad is cola-coloured urine (haematuria), hypertension and oliguria (RFT impairment). (Book p775)]

Which feature is NOT part of the PSGN triad shown in the book's triangle figure? [Pulmonary oedema is listed under 'other features', not in the triad of haematuria, hypertension and oliguria. (Book p775)]

Diastolic BP fluctuation in PSGN raises the risk of PRES, which then may cause: [Diastolic BP fluctuation → increased risk of PRES (posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome)/hypertensive encephalopathy → seizures. (Book p775)]

Fill up: In PSGN, the abbreviation PRES stands for posterior reversible ______ syndrome. [PRES = posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, the consequence of diastolic BP fluctuation/hypertensive encephalopathy in PSGN. (Book p775)]

Pulmonary oedema and hyperkalaemia are listed among the 'other features' of acute PSGN, separate from the classical triad. [Other features of acute PSGN: pulmonary oedema, hyperkalaemia and diastolic BP fluctuation with PRES/hypertensive encephalopathy and seizures. (Book p]

elements.source: Complete the pathogenesis flowchart of hypertension and pulmonary oedema in PSGN — 1) NAPlr + plasmin  2) ENaC  3) Na⁺ and H₂O retention … A) Activates the channel  B) End result: hypertension and pulmonary oedema  C) Epithelial sodium channel that is activated [Flowchart: NAPlr + plasmin → activates ENaC (epithelial Na⁺ channel) → retention of Na⁺ and H₂O → hypertension and pulmonary oedema. (Book p776)]

The channel activated by the NAPlr–plasmin complex in PSGN is: [NAPlr + plasmin activates ENaC (epithelial Na⁺ channel), causing sodium and water retention that explains hypertension and pulmonary oedema. (Book p77]
Fill up: NAPlr bound to ______ activates ENaC in PSGN. [NAPlr + plasmin activates the epithelial Na⁺ channel (ENaC). (Book p776)]

In PSGN, volume-dependent hypertension and pulmonary oedema are attributed to ENaC-mediated retention of sodium and water. [The pathogenesis chart links NAPlr-plasmin → ENaC activation → Na⁺/H₂O retention → hypertension and pulmonary oedema. (Book p776)]
Renal function tests in PSGN typically show: [Basic investigations: RFT shows mild impairment, matching the reversible oliguric picture of PSGN. (Book p776)]

A 6-year-old with PSGN has the following urinalysis: RBCs 3+, albumin 1+, and white cell casts on microscopy. This picture is: [Urine examination in PSGN: ↑↑ RBC, albumin 1+/2+, and WBC casts. (Book p776)]

A child with PSGN has a persistently low C3 beyond 8 weeks. The book's stated action is: [Biopsy indication: ↓C3 persisting beyond 8 weeks — likely C3 GN (serum C3 normally normalises by 8 weeks in PSGN). (Book p776)]

A second episode of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is common and simply needs a repeat course of penicillin. [Biopsy indication 2: recurrent episode — PSGN does not recur, hence an alternative diagnosis must be evaluated. (Book p776)]
The histopathology of PSGN is best described as: [Histopathology in PSGN: DPGN (diffuse proliferative GN) with exudative neutrophilic capillary infiltration > mesangial proliferation. (Book p776)]

Fill up: The histopathology of PSGN is abbreviated DPGN, i.e. diffuse ______ glomerulonephritis. [DPGN = diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis, with neutrophils in capillary loops exceeding mesangial proliferation. (Book p776)]

Match the immunopathology with its PSGN phase — 1) Clinical phase on immunofluorescence  2) Recovery phase on immunofluorescence  3) Electron microscopy … A) Subepithelial camel-hump deposits  B) Only C3 in the mesangium  C) Granular IgG ± C3 in capillary walls > mesangium [IF: clinical phase = granular IgG ± C3 in capillary walls more than mesangium (starry sky); recovery phase = only C3 (mesangial). EM: subepithelial ca]

A renal biopsy from a child in the recovery phase of PSGN is stained for immunofluorescence. Which deposit pattern is expected now? [Recovery phase IF: only C3 (mesangial); the granular IgG + C3 capillary-wall pattern belongs to the clinical phase. (Book p776)]

A 7-year-old with PSGN has a BP of 150/100 mmHg. According to the treatment table, the drug of choice and its dose are: [Hypertension in PSGN: calcium channel blockers (amlodipine 2.5–5 mg) with BP charting hourly. (Book p776)]
The amlodipine dose printed in the PSGN treatment table is: [Hypertension in PSGN is treated with the CCB amlodipine 2.5–5 mg, with BP charted hourly. (Book p776)]
A child with acute PSGN develops pulmonary oedema. The table's treatment is: [Pulmonary oedema in PSGN: diuretics, such as torsemide 5–10 mg. (Book p776)]
The listed dose of torsemide for pulmonary oedema in PSGN is: [Pulmonary oedema in PSGN is treated with diuretics — torsemide 5–10 mg. (Book p776)]

A child with PSGN has a serum potassium of 6.6 mEq/L. Per the treatment table, the monitoring that must accompany this is: [Hyperkalaemia (which can cause cardiac complications) in PSGN: ECG monitoring — check for tall T waves — and serum K⁺ checked regularly. (Book p776)]

Match each sign in the PSGN treatment table with its prescription — 1) Hypertension  2) Pulmonary oedema  3) Hyperkalaemia … A) Torsemide 5–10 mg  B) ECG monitoring and serial serum K⁺  C) Amlodipine 2.5–5 mg with hourly BP charting [Treatment table: hypertension → CCB amlodipine 2.5–5 mg + hourly BP charting; pulmonary oedema → diuretic torsemide 5–10 mg; hyperkalaemia → ECG monit]

The ECG change specifically named for hyperkalaemia in the PSGN treatment table is the tall T wave. [Hyperkalaemia row: ECG monitoring (check for tall T waves) and serum K⁺ levels checked regularly. (Book p776)]

The histopathology figure labelled 'DPGN histopathology' on this page illustrates: [The figure shows a light-microscopy image of DPGN (diffuse proliferative GN) — the characteristic histopathology of PSGN. (Book p776)]

An immunofluorescence image in a child with acute PSGN is reported as a 'starry sky pattern'. This corresponds to: [Clinical-phase IF in PSGN: granular IgG ± C3 in capillary walls > mesangium, described as the starry sky pattern (figure 'IF: starry sky pattern'). (B]

Which immunofluorescence pattern is NOT part of the described PSGN findings? [Linear IgG along the GBM indicates anti-GBM (Goodpasture/RPGN type I) disease, not PSGN, whose IF is granular in the clinical phase and mesangial C3-o]

elements.source: What is the indication for antibiotics in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis? [Antibiotics in PSGN are indicated for an active sore throat; they do not alter the course of the established glomerulonephritis. (Book p777)]

Match the antibiotic regimen for an active sore throat — 1) Benzathine penicillin  2) Oral penicillin V  3) Penicillin allergy … A) 500 mg BD for 5–10 days  B) Erythromycin  C) Single dose of 1.2 million units [Regimens: single-dose benzathine penicillin 1.2 million units; oral penicillin V 500 mg BD × 5–10 days; erythromycin when penicillin-allergic. (Book p]

The single dose of benzathine penicillin used for an active sore throat in PSGN is: [Single-dose benzathine penicillin 1.2 million units is one of the listed options for an active sore throat. (Book p777)]
Oral penicillin V for an active sore throat in PSGN is given as 500 mg twice daily for: [Oral penicillin V: 500 mg BD × 5–10 days, as an alternative to single-dose benzathine penicillin. (Book p777)]
Fill up: In penicillin allergy with an active sore throat, the antibiotic listed is ______. [In penicillin allergy, erythromycin is the listed antibiotic for an active sore throat. (Book p777)]

The note on this page states that nephrotic syndrome shows no pulmonary oedema. [Note: 'Nephrotic syndrome: no pulmonary oedema' — contrasting the intravascular-volume depletion of nephrotic syndrome with the volume overload of the]
With prompt treatment, what percentage of PSGN patients recover in 3–5 days? [Recovery: 99% recover in 3–5 days with prompt treatment. (Book p777)]

Six months after an episode of PSGN, a boy still has 5–10 RBCs/hpf on urine microscopy but normal BP, creatinine and serum C3. What is the correct advice? [Recovery point 2: microhaematuria can persist after treatment and has no significance — unlike the persistent ↓C3 (>8 weeks) that would warrant biopsy]

A 6-year-old treated for PSGN is reviewed at 8 weeks: haematuria persists but serum C3 has normalised. The correct interpretation is: [Recovery point: 99% recover in 3-5 days with prompt treatment, and microhaematuria may persist after treatment with no significance; follow-up is by s]
Follow-up after an episode of PSGN is done with: [Follow-up: serum C3, expected to be normal after 8 weeks; persistence beyond 8 weeks suggests C3 GN and needs biopsy. (Book p777)]
In the management of PIGN/IRGN, serum C3 is low in what proportion of patients? [Investigations in PIGN/IRGN: serum C3 is low in 60% of patients (in contrast to 90% in PSGN). (Book p777)]
The biopsy findings described for PIGN/IRGN are: [PIGN/IRGN biopsy: IgA-predominant ± C3, or C3-predominant deposits showing a garland/rope pattern. (Book p777)]

A 5-year-old with post-streptococcal GN has C3 measured at presentation, and his cousin with MRSA-related infection-associated GN is also tested. The expected results are: [PSGN shows a low C3 in 90% of patients; for PIGN/IRGN the text states a low C3 in 60% of patients, while the p775 table prints '↑C3 (in 60%)' — learn ]

A renal biopsy from a patient with staphylococcal infection-related GN shows C3-dominant deposits arranged in an arc around the glomerular capillary wall. This appearance is called: [PIGN/IRGN biopsy shows IgA-predominant ± C3 or C3-predominant deposits in a garland/rope pattern. (Book p777)]
The prognosis and management described for PIGN/IRGN are: [Treatment section: poor prognosis; vancomycin (nephrotoxic) and dialysis are listed. (Book p777)]

Steroids are the mainstay of treatment for PIGN/IRGN, while antibiotics reliably reverse the RPGN. [The note states that steroids worsen cellulitis and that other antibiotics do not treat the RPGN of PIGN/IRGN — hence the poor prognosis. (Book p777)]

Which of the following is NOT listed in the treatment of PIGN/IRGN? [Treatment listed for PIGN/IRGN is vancomycin (nephrotoxic) plus dialysis; steroids are specifically warned against because they worsen cellulitis. (Bo]

Fill up: In PIGN/IRGN the antibiotic named in treatment is ______, which is nephrotoxic. [Treatment of PIGN/IRGN includes vancomycin, noted to be nephrotoxic, along with dialysis for the renal failure. (Book p777)]

Match the onset and oedema of the nephrotic versus nephritic table — 1) Nephrotic onset  2) Nephritic onset  3) Nephrotic oedema compartment … A) Extravascular (+++)  B) Insidious  C) Abrupt [Table rows: onset is insidious in nephrotic and abrupt in nephritic syndrome; nephrotic oedema is extravascular (+++) whereas nephritic oedema is intr]

Match the BP and JVP entries of the nephrotic versus nephritic table — 1) Nephrotic BP  2) Nephritic BP  3) Nephritic JVP … A) Raised  B) Normal  C) High [In the table, nephrotic syndrome has a normal BP and normal JVP, while nephritic syndrome has a high BP with a raised JVP (intravascular volume expans]

Regarding proteinuria, haematuria and casts in the nephrotic versus nephritic table, which statement is correct? [Table: proteinuria more, haematuria less and RBC casts absent in nephrotic syndrome; proteinuria less, haematuria more and RBC casts present in nephri]

A 4-year-old has generalised pitting oedema, BP 95/60 mmHg, normal JVP and 4+ proteinuria with no RBC casts. Serum albumin is low. Which syndrome does this describe? [Nephrotic syndrome: insidious onset, extravascular (+++) oedema, normal BP and JVP, more proteinuria, less haematuria, absent RBC casts and low serum ]

A 7-year-old presents with cola-coloured urine, BP 140/95 mmHg and raised JVP, with 1+ albuminuria and RBC casts; serum albumin is 3.9 g/dL. Which syndrome is this? [Nephritic syndrome: abrupt onset, high BP, raised JVP (intravascular ++ oedema), less proteinuria, more haematuria, RBC casts present and normal or sl]

Which serum albumin finding belongs to nephrotic syndrome and NOT to nephritic syndrome? [Serum albumin is low in nephrotic syndrome, whereas in nephritic syndrome it is normal or only slightly decreased. (Book p777)]
Fill up: In the nephrotic vs nephritic table, the oedema of nephrotic syndrome is mainly ______. [Oedema: nephrotic = extravascular (+++); nephritic = intravascular (++). (Book p777)]

RBC casts are a feature of the nephritic syndrome and are absent in nephrotic syndrome. [The table lists RBC casts as absent (–) in nephrotic syndrome and present (+) in nephritic syndrome. (Book p777)]
Comparing proteinuria and haematuria, the nephritic syndrome is characterised by: [Nephritic: proteinuria less, haematuria more. Nephrotic: proteinuria more, haematuria less. (Book p777)]
